query: For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the onset or suppression of corrosion-related degradation in harsh environments at room and elevated temperatures? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to the untreated reference, applicable boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: Residual stresses induced during rapid plasma spraying of an HEA coating onto pre-exposed Q235 steel promote microcrack formation that accelerates localized corrosion; applying a controlled post-deposition low-temperature annealing treatment relieves these stresses and suppresses degradation.
generation.material_initial_state: Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state (with native oxide and controlled surface finish) having been plasma-sprayed with a HEA (e.g., CoCrFeNiMo-based alloy) that exhibits high residual tensile stresses and minor microcracks.
generation.intervention: Implement a controlled thermal-relaxation (annealing) treatment (e.g., 300°C for 1 hour under inert atmosphere) immediately post-spraying to relieve residual stresses without triggering deleterious phase changes.
generation.conditions: Exposure to 3.5 wt% NaCl solution and simulated geothermal fluid at room temperature and moderately elevated temperatures (60–80°C) to mimic service environments.
generation.structural_mediator: Reduction in microcrack density and defect concentration within the HEA coating and at the coating/substrate interface.
generation.mechanism: High residual stresses from rapid plasma deposition induce microcracking, which creates pathways for corrosive species; annealing relieves these stresses, healing microcracks and improving coating integrity, thereby reducing localized corrosion initiation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Annealed coatings will exhibit significantly lower corrosion rates, fewer microcracks, and enhanced electrochemical impedance (indicative of a more protective surface) compared to as-sprayed, unannealed coatings.
generation.baseline: Q235 steel with the as-sprayed HEA coating (no post-deposition stress-relief treatment).
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is confined to coatings produced under conditions where initial residual stress is high and the annealing cycle is optimized to avoid unwanted microstructural coarsening or phase transformations.
generation.uncertainty: While stress relief is expected to reduce corrosion, the influence of the Q235 steel’s pre-existing native oxide and surface irregularities on overall adhesion and long-term corrosion behavior remains partly uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of plasma-sprayed HEA coatings on Q235 steel (ensuring similar pre-exposure surface conditions): one set left as-sprayed and one set subjected to the defined annealing treatment. Expose both sets to the same corrosive environments.
measurements: Residual stress evaluations using XRD sin²ψ method pre- and post-annealing
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) and potentiodynamic polarization tests to compare corrosion parameters
Microscopic (SEM) inspection to quantify microcrack density and morphology
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If post-annealing coatings do not demonstrate statistically significant improvements in corrosion resistance (e.g., no reduction in corrosion current density or microcrack density compared to as-sprayed samples), then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: (1) The (CoCrFeNi)95Nb5 HEA coating was prepared by plasma spraying on substrate of the Q235 steel, consisting of a simple FCC solid solution with Laves phase, and the coating bonded well to the substrate. (2) Elemental segregation occurred between the dendrites and the interdendrites of the coating, and the elements Cr and Nb with high melting point were enriched between the interdendrites. This phenomenon may be due to the difference in melting point of the element and the characteristics of the plasma spraying process. (3) The coating has a microhardness of 321 HV0.5, which can effectively improve the surface hardness of the Q235 steel part. (4) The (CoCrFeNi)95Nb5 HEA coating exhibited excellent corrosion resistance in the electrochemical corrosion test of a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution comparing to previously studied coatings prepared by other processes. (5) In the 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution, the selective corrosion occurred on the surface of (CoCrFeNi)95Nb5 HEA coating, while the interdendritic phase rich in Nb and Cr was preferentially corroded as an anode, and the dendritic phase rich in Co, Ni, and Fe was protected as a cathode.

One of the properties that are sought after in the production of HEAs is enhanced mechanical strength of the material, which, in an addition to good corrosion resistance properties, can make the HEAs an optimal selection for a material application in a harsh, erosive-corrosive environment [,,]. In the light of HEA application via LMD technology for geothermal applications, substrates such as carbon steels and stainless steels could be employed to evaluate the protection of components such as piping, casing, steam turbine, etc. For instance, it is well known that carbon steel application within the geothermal field involves a thick material wall design required to account for a uniform thinning (due to corrosion) of the material. Due to the enhanced performance of HEAs, the application of LMD coated HEAs on carbon steel could therefore reduce the corrosion rate and hence reduce material wall thickness requirements. Furthermore, the application of HEA coating could also extend the lifetime of the equipment in the corrosive geothermal environment.
